web_title: 0. Executive Thesis, Dual Verdict & Opportunity Matrix
question: Why did Stallion move from a waiting posture on 13 November to a hard rejection on 25 November 2026, and what would it take to reconsider?

web_blocks.html: Stallion India Fluorochemicals is downgraded from a waiting posture to a hard rejection for new capital. November 2026 filings broke the pillars that kept the stock on our watchlist. Monitoring-agency reports, a GST Section 67 search notice, and SEBI insider-sale records exposed severe control and cash gaps [36][37][38][39][40]. Both flagship plants slipped out of FY27 with cost overruns [36][37][38]. Core operating margins fell below 10% while integrated rivals earned 25% to 34% [36][42][43][44]. Operating cash flow relapsed to −₹39.17 crore [36]. On 25 November live TradingView, the stock broke its 200-day average to ₹171.59, down from ₹180.48 on the 23 November NSE ledger [32].

We anchor our refreshed verdict, FY28 targets, and chart levels across both dated sessions. The 23 November 2026 NSE ledger closed at ₹180.48, while the 25 November live TradingView close fell to ₹171.59 [14][32][36].

web_blocks.takeaway: Every core pillar moved against Stallion since 13 November: KPI health failed, FY28 base value dropped from ₹233.4 to ₹143.2, and the 200-day average broke decisively.

web_blocks.html: The action for your portfolio is simple. Stallion is not held in any account, so there is nothing to sell. New capital stays completely out at ₹171.59. It also stays out if the stock drops to the ₹155.07 to ₹159.79 pivot shelf. Once we remove spent cash and price governance risk honestly, fair value drops below that shelf. Both our FY28 base target (₹143.2) and weighted value (₹132.9) imply a loss even from technical support.

Our prior dossier left three open questions: why Q2 margins hit 2.20%, why promoter stake fell 20.1 points, and whether Bhilwara would start on time. November filings answered all three, and each answer broke bearish. First, a ₹9.51 crore ESOP catch-up drove part of Q2's drop, yet core margin ex-ESOP and treasury income still fell 557 bps to 9.19% [36]. In that same quarter, Navin Fluorine, Gujarat Fluorochemicals, and SRF earned 25% to 34% margins [42][43][44]. Second, SEBI SAST filings showed the CEO sold 3.06% in late 2025 before taking minimal rights shares [40]. Promoter stake fell from 67.90% to 47.80%, while institutional holding dropped to 1.88% [15]. Third, Bhilwara slipped seven months to April–May 2027 with a ₹40 crore overrun, and Mambattu slipped to early FY28 [36][37][38]. Neither plant adds FY27 sales. Management now flags a third ₹200 crore raise and called cash flow not a true reflection of anything [36].
We test Stallion across short-term trading, medium-term inflection, and long-term compounding. That split shows whether any holding period warrants capital today [32][36][37][38].

book_paragraphs: Here is the answer before the evidence, and I want to state the downgrade plainly. On 13 November 2026, we placed Stallion India Fluorochemicals on a waiting list for its support zone. Twelve days later, after reading the November filings, monitoring-agency reports, GST search disclosure, and live technical breakdown, we are downgrading Stallion to a hard rejection for new capital—Tier 0 conviction, zero percent allocation across every holding horizon.

Nothing in investing is more dangerous than clinging to an old support price after the business underneath it cracks. On 13 November, three crucial questions were still unanswered: why September's operating margin collapsed to 2.2%, why promoter ownership dropped twenty percentage points in six months, and whether the flagship Bhilwara R-32 plant would actually start by December 2026. Over the past two weeks, primary regulatory filings answered all three questions, and every single answer broke sharply against minority shareholders.

First, operational execution slipped again across both expansion projects. While the Khalapur high-purity helium facility did begin commercial operations on 21 September 2026—334 days behind its IPO prospectus date, with standalone helium revenue still undisclosed—both Bhilwara R-32 and Mambattu slipped out of FY27 completely. Infomerics logged a seven-month delay at Bhilwara to March 2027, and on the 19 November call management confirmed trials in March, phased production in April, stabilization in May, zero FY27 revenue, and a 40 crore cost overrun. CARE Ratings confirmed Mambattu breached two prior deadlines and slipped into early FY28 with nearly doubled cost scope and zero FY27 revenue.

Second, earnings quality deteriorated far beyond the ESOP headline. Management pointed to a 9.51 crore two-quarter non-cash ESOP catch-up to explain September's weak profit, with another 4.7 crore per quarter still coming in the second half. Yet even stripping out ESOPs and removing 3.34 crore of treasury other income, core operating margin fell 557 basis points year on year to 9.19%. In that exact same quarter, backward-integrated Indian rivals Navin Fluorine, Gujarat Fluorochemicals, and SRF posted 25% to 34% margins on R-32 and won a five-year DGTR recommendation to keep anti-dumping duties on Chinese R-32—a tariff wall that boosts integrated rivals while squeezing Stallion's China-import blending spreads.

Third, cash flow and governance broke simultaneously. First-half FY27 operating cash flow relapsed to negative 39.17 crore despite 30.53 crore of pre-tax profit. Cash and bank balances shrank 142 crore in six months as 129 crore moved into unmapped on-account advances to civil contractor Pansen Engineering under a cost-plus-10% contract before invoicing. CARE Ratings formally qualified the IPO monitoring report for object deviation, fund commingling across routine bank accounts, and misclassified issue expenses. Infomerics documented 36 crore—nearly ten percent of the gross rights issue—spent on issue expenses. Maharashtra GST officials conducted a six-day Section 67 search in October flagging five Input Tax Credit contraventions, settled without disclosing the rupee outflow. SEBI filings proved the Chairman and CEO sold 3.06% of the company in the open market in late 2025 before barely participating in the February 2026 rights issue, dropping promoter stake from 67.90% to 47.80% while institutional ownership collapsed to 1.88%. And after raising 525 crore across two equity issues in fourteen months, management signaled a third 200 crore fundraise while the CEO declared on the call—with no CFO present—that cash flow is not a true reflection of anything.

Fourth, both valuation and the tape confirm the rejection. Keep both verified dates clear: Stallion closed at 180.48 rupees on the 23 November NSE market-facts ledger, then fell another 4.93% to 171.59 rupees on the 25 November live TradingView close, decisively breaking its 200-day simple moving average at 183.54 rupees into a Stage 4 downtrend. At 171.59 rupees, Stallion still trades at 39.6 times on TradingView and 43.6 to 46.2 times on Screener—more expensive than integrated industry leader SRF at 32.7 times. Once we stop double-counting bank cash that is already committed to finishing plants and funding working capital, our re-underwritten FY28 base value drops from 233.4 rupees to 143.2 rupees, and our probability-weighted two-year fair value drops to 132.9 rupees—down 22.5% from today's price, and still negative even from the 155 to 160 rupee support shelf. Add potential equity dilution from the signaled 200 crore raise and weighted fair value falls to 117.7 rupees.

Because Stallion is not held in any account in our ledger, there are zero shares to sell. One hundred percent of the next marginal rupee stays in cash. Every chapter that follows documents the filings, the peer divergence, the re-underwritten arithmetic, and the broken Stage 4 tape that drove this downgrade—alongside the exact four-part evidence bar Stallion would have to clear before earning a second look.
